title: Make the scheduler's task list fail fast

blocks.text: The scheduler keeps the tasks due on each tick in `DueTasks`, a small array-backed list. Its plugins walk the list, and some of them change it while they walk: they drop a task they have handled, or add a follow-up. Last week a plugin dropped a task mid-walk, and the walk silently skipped the task after it. The team wants a walk that might skip or repeat a task to throw instead, and a plugin that changes the list through its own walk to keep going without either.
`add`, `removeAt`, `set` and the counter `modCount` are written. Finish the two `TODO` methods of the nested `Walk` class in `src/main/java/practice/DueTasks.java`:

items: `next()`: the next task id, or `ConcurrentModificationException` when the list changed behind the walk's back;
`remove()`: removes the id `next()` just returned, and leaves the walk able to carry on.

cases.says: a walk returns every task in the order it was added
replacing a task in place during a walk does not stop the walk, which returns the new id
a walk can remove its last task through itself
a task added to the list behind the walk's back makes the walk's next step throw ConcurrentModificationException
a removal and an add behind the walk's back, which leave the size unchanged, still make the next step throw
after removing a task through itself, the walk carries on without throwing and returns every remaining task
removing two neighbouring tasks through the walk visits and removes both, skipping neither

origin.section: A Fail-Fast Iterator Checks a Counter on Every Step, and One Thread Is Enough to Trip It

concepts: Iterator.remove() removes the element next() returned and resynchronises the iterator, so the walk carries on without skipping or throwing.
A fail-fast iterator copies the collection's structural-change counter when created and throws ConcurrentModificationException from the next step once the counter has moved.
Replacing a value (set, entry.setValue, put of an existing key) is not structural and does not trip a fail-fast iterator.
